newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK data may overstate jobs mkt tightness.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK data may overstate jobs mkt tightness.

text.p: UK jobs data for September due on Wednesday are set to show unemployment stuck at 7.5 percent for the second month running, a level not seen since 1987 when wages started to spiral upward.
But the unemployment rate could be overstating the tightness of the labour market as it has been affected by a decline in the participation rate in recent years.
In addition, increased flexibility in the labour market, the prevelance of part-time work and short-term contracts, has weakened the link between labour market tightness and wage pressures.

"The labour market is clearly tightening -- hardly surprising given the stage of the economic cycle -- but only slowly and certainly not fast enough to place upward pressure on wages," said Jonathan Loynes.

The Reuters consensus forecast suggests unemployment fell 20,000 in September after a fall of 15,600 in August. Average earnings in August are forecast to stay unchanged at 3.75 percent. The figures are due at 0830 GMT on Wednesday.
Gauging the level of labour market tightness has not been helped by the suspiciously high level of job centre vacancies.
They have surged by 53,000, or 29.2 percent, in the last year, is the biggest annual rise since 1987.

The Office for National Statisics (ONS) warned the introduction of a new computer system at Job Centres has resulted in a large number of job vacancies being left on the system after they have been filled.

"This would explain why the latest rise in vacancies has been due entirely to a fall in the number of vacancy outflows," said Loynes. "This is the opposite to the pattern normally witnessed during periods of stronger activity when a rise of inflows provided the momentum."
Vacancy inflows have actually fallen back in the recently.
Added to this is uncertainty over the true size of labour supply. Some discouraged workers who left the workforce in the last few years may be willing to rejoin when activity picks up.
This has allowed the Bank of England to be uncharacteristically relaxed about labour market tightness.
In its most recent inflation report, it said one possible explanation for the subdued wage behaviour in the current recovery is the lower natural rate of employment than in the previous cycle.

"It is possible that the natural state of unemployment is lower now than it was in the late 1980s. Measure of labour market tightness which take into account hours worked suggest the labour market has not tightened since the middle of last year," it concluded.
But other economists said it would be dangerous for employers to rely on the economically inactive to ease labour shortages if economic activity picks up pace.

"The decline in the participation rate is most marked among the young and old," said David Mackie, UK economist at JP Morgan. "The group aged between 25 and 49 has seen very little change in the participation rate which suggests changes are more structural than cycical."

The sharpest fall in participation is among young adults aged 16-19 and 20-24 as they tend to stay in education for longer. Their participation has fallen by 10.2 percent and 5.9 percent respectively since the spring of 1990.

And the propensity to retire early has affected the group aged between 50 and 64. It participation has fallen by 1.5 percent. "It would be surprising if the cyclical upswing in the coming eighteen months reversed either of these structural changes," said Mackie. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7715
